newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Credit Suisse plunges into 1996 loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Credit Suisse plunges into 1996 loss.

text.p: Credit Suisse Group said on Wednesday it plunged to a 1996 net loss after minority interests of 2.59 billion Swiss francs ($1.7 billion) due to extraordinary charges of 5.4 billion francs for restructuring and providing for bad loans.
But based on what Credit Suisse described as "a gratifying start to the current year," the bank's management decided to pay an unchanged dividend of four francs per share.
The loss, the first in the group's 140-year history, was above the 2.1 billion franc deficit it had forecast late last year.
The difference is due to a 195 million franc increase in general reserves for banking risks as well as a decision not to activate 170 million francs in U.S. losses for tax purposes.
Last December Credit Suisse said the loss would be one of the results of a 3.9 billion franc extraordinary charge linked with a sweeping change in the way it makes provisions for credit losses.
Credit Suisse executives also said 1997 had begun on a positive note, but they were wary of making any strong statements about the outlook for this year.
Chief executive Lukas Muehlemann said business got off to a good start "but one cannot assume that the entire year will go as well as the first two months".

Muehlemann, newly hired from Swiss Reinsurance, told a news conference that Credit Suisse expected structural improvements in its earnings during 1997. "For the current year Credit Suisse Group expects structural improvements in earning power throughout the group and, in particular, in Swiss business," he said.

Muehlemann also said the group was not yet satisfied with the performance of its private banking operations, but was convinced that its earnings target of 40 to 50 basis points on funds under management was a "very realistic goal".

The group's return on equity goal was 15 percent, the goal for its Credit Suisse retail banking unit was 10 to 12 percent, the target for Credit Suisse First Boston was more than 15 percent and for its asset management arm the target was 12 to 15 percent, he said.

Separately, Credit Suisse executives said broad restructuring measures taken last year led to a 161 million franc loss in its domestic trading operations. Net trading profits for the group were up 33 percent to 3.901 billion francs.
Shares in Credit Suisse were down 0.75 francs in late afternoon trading at 157.75 francs.
Credit Suisse, along with Switzerland's two other major banks, Union Bank of Switzerland and Swiss Bank Corp., last year changed their method for calculating provisions for loans.
Swiss banks have been hard hit by the long-running downturn in the Swiss economy and have had to write-off billions of francs in bad loans in recent years.

As part of its new strategy Credit Suisse also embarked on a lrestructuring that involved dropping the name of CS Holding from the group and creating four new operational units -- retail banking, private banking, investment banking and asset management.

Apart from the extraordinary charges, Credit Suisse's operating results last year improved slightly with pre-tax operating profit rising three percent to 2.47 billion francs. Gross earnings from normal banking business rose 17 percent to 12.89 billion francs with trading income soaring 33 percent to 3.9 billion.

Profits from trading such instruments as currencies, shares or metals accounted for roughly one third of total gross earnings while interest business accounted for 27 percent. ($ = 1.481 Swiss Francs)
